augustine-will: Augustine observed that a single person can will two opposite things at once — wanting to change while still clinging to what needs changing — and called this a divided will. On his view, moral evil begins not in some outside force but in a will that loves good things in the wrong order. Many later thinkers use his picture of inner conflict to explain why we fail to do what we ourselves endorse.
being-toward-death: This is Heidegger's term for the way human existence is shaped by anticipating its own death. Death, for him, is not just a future event to schedule around but the ultimate limit that makes each life irreducibly one's own. Many hold that facing mortality squarely — rather than fleeing it in everyday busyness and small talk — is what allows a person to live authentically.
dasein: Dasein is Heidegger's label for the kind of being that we are — literally, 'being-there.' It names a creature that does not simply exist among things but understands and cares about its own existence, always already involved in a world of purposes, tools, and other people. Heidegger coined the term to replace the detached 'subject' of older philosophy with an engaged, situated self.
dewey-experience: John Dewey argued that genuine experience — doing something, undergoing its consequences, and connecting the two — is the root of both learning and art. Education should grow out of lived experience rather than rote absorption, and an artwork, likewise, is not a static object but an experience that completes itself in the one having it. Well-shaped experience, for Dewey, is what makes growth continuous.
hegel-history: Hegel proposed that history is not one thing after another but a directional process: through the clash of opposing ideas and ways of life, human consciousness gradually comes to understand — and to actualize — freedom. Each era's conflicts, on this view, push humanity a step further. Many find the grand pattern compelling; others see it as a speculative story imposed on messy events.
heidegger-technology: Heidegger argued that modern technology is not just a collection of tools but a way of thinking that reveals the whole world — rivers, forests, even human minds — as 'standing reserve': raw material waiting to be optimized and used. The danger is that we, too, come to see ourselves as resources. Yet recognizing this framing, he held, is the first step toward a freer relation with our devices.
hume-induction: Hume pointed out that all our expectations about the unobserved — that the sun will rise, that bread will nourish — rest on the assumption that nature keeps behaving as it has so far. But no argument can prove that assumption without circularly assuming it. His problem of induction still challenges philosophers: our confidence in scientific generalization may be reasonable habit, yet it is not demonstrable proof.
just-war-theory: Just war theory holds that war can sometimes be morally permissible, but only under strict conditions. Going to war requires a just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, proportionality, and last resort; even a justified war must be fought by rules — sparing civilians, using no more force than necessary. Traced to Augustine and Aquinas and refined ever since, it aims to bind warfare to justice.
kant-aesthetics: Kant analyzed two distinctive aesthetic experiences. A judgment of taste rests on disinterested pleasure — liking something for how it looks or sounds, not for what it does for us — yet we speak as if everyone ought to agree. The sublime is the mixed awe and dread we feel before overwhelming vastness or power, from which Kant thought we derive a strange satisfaction: discovering that our rational self outranks mere nature.
land-ethic: Aldo Leopold's land ethic enlarges the moral community to include soils, waters, plants, and animals — the land as a whole — not just humans and, at most, individual animals. On this view we are plain members of a biotic community rather than its conquerors, and an action is right insofar as it preserves that community's integrity. The idea remains a touchstone of environmental ethics.
monadology: Leibniz's Monadology claims that reality is built from monads: simple, indivisible, mind-like substances that have, as he put it, no windows and cannot causally touch one another. Each monad perceives the universe from its own point of view, and their apparent interactions are coordinated by a harmony established in advance. The theory is an audacious answer to how a world of many things can still be one ordered whole.
nietzsche-perspectivism: Nietzsche's perspectivism holds that we never grasp the world from nowhere: every claim, theory, and value expresses some particular standpoint, interest, and way of life. His notorious suggestion that there are 'no facts, only interpretations' is often read not as anything-goes relativism but as a demand for honesty about one's standpoint. Many interpreters stress that perspectives can still be compared and ranked against each other.
noble-lie: In Plato's Republic, the rulers of the ideal city tell citizens a beneficial myth — the 'noble lie' — to secure social harmony, convincing people of a shared origin that fits them to their stations. The phrase now names any falsehood told, usually by authority, for what its teller takes to be the public good. It still frames debates over propaganda, paternalism, and whether some lies serve higher ends.
ontological-argument: Anselm's ontological argument tries to prove God's existence from the concept of God alone. Define God as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived,' Anselm reasons, and since existing in reality is greater than existing merely in the mind, such a being must exist. Critics from Gaunilo to Kant have doubted that existence can be defined into anything; modern modal versions keep the debate alive.
personalism: Personalism is the family of views holding that the person — unique, self-conscious, capable of free choice and love — is the highest kind of value and must never be treated as a mere thing. Thinkers from Borden Parker Bowne to Max Scheler and Martin Buber developed it, and it informed Martin Luther King Jr.'s social ethics. Institutions, on this view, exist for persons, not the reverse.
phenomenology: Phenomenology is the philosophical study of experience as it is lived: what perceiving, remembering, dreaming, or acting is like from the inside, and how objects show up within them. Husserl urged setting aside our assumptions about the external world in order to describe consciousness carefully, noting that awareness is always awareness of something. Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty later embedded the experiencer in a world and a body.
pragmatic-truth: The pragmatist conception of truth, associated with William James, holds that a belief's truth is bound up with its practical success: true ideas are those we can verify, that guide us fruitfully, that 'work' within experience. Critics object that this confuses truth with usefulness, since a comforting falsehood still fails to match reality. Defenders reply that correspondence itself is known only through inquiry's results.
sophist-relativism: The Sophist Protagoras taught that 'man is the measure of all things': what seems true or just to each person — or each city — is true or just for them, with no higher standard above. This ancient relativism, and the Sophists' skill at making weaker arguments look stronger, drew Socrates' and Plato's fierce opposition, and it still anchors debates over whether truth is objective or made by communities.
speciesism: Speciesism, a term popularized by Peter Singer, names the supposed prejudice of giving weight to a being's interests merely because of its species, as racism does with race. Singer argues that suffering counts equally wherever it occurs, so factory farming and animal experimentation stand condemned alongside analogous treatment of humans. Critics reply that species membership can itself ground moral differences, and the debate remains unresolved.
stoic-cosmopolitanism: Stoic cosmopolitanism is the ancient Stoic idea that each of us is a citizen not of one city but of the world, bound to all rational beings by shared reason. Hierocles imagined concentric circles of concern — self, family, city, humanity — and urged shrinking them inward until strangers count as kin. The view underwrites the ideal of universal human fellowship and later natural-rights thinking.
stoic-present-moment: The Stoics held that the present moment is all we ever truly possess: the past is gone, the future uncertain, and both exist only as memory and anticipation, which regret and fear inflate. Seneca argued that life is not short — we squander it by deferring living — and Marcus Aurelius trained himself to attend to the task at hand. Presence, for them, was a discipline rather than a mood.
taoism: Taoism (Daoism) is a Chinese philosophical tradition centered on the Dao — the Way — the spontaneous, unnameable pattern underlying nature. The Daodejing counsels wu wei, acting effortlessly and without forcing, in accord with things' own tendencies, while Zhuangzi's stories celebrate free wandering and the relativity of viewpoints. Its ideals of simplicity, suppleness, and harmony with nature have shaped Eastern thought for millennia.
turing-test: Alan Turing proposed replacing the vague question 'can machines think?' with an operational test: if, in a blind conversation, a machine's responses are indistinguishable from a human's, we should credit it with intelligence. The test judges mind by behavior and ability, not by inner mechanism. Critics, most famously John Searle, object that fluent performance proves no understanding — a dispute that still divides philosophers of mind.
williams-integrity: Bernard Williams attacked utilitarianism for what he saw as its threat to integrity. In his famous cases, a utilitarian calculation makes one person's own hand in wrongdoing — killing one to save others — no worse than letting the harm happen, dissolving the difference between what I do and what merely happens through me. Our deepest commitments, Williams argued, are not interchangeable counters but what make a life ours.
